moduleTitle: Managing application access for Business Architects (Roles and Personas)
learningObjectives: Differentiate between a user and a Persona in a Pega application.
Explain the relationship between Personas, operator record, Access Groups, and Access Roles.
Differentiate between authorization and authentication in relation to application security.

elements.description: Two levels of identity in Pega access control:
items: USER (operator) — an individual person who interacts with the application
PERSONA — a CATEGORY (role) grouping users with similar access needs, goals, and channels

elements.description: Each user has an Operator ID record that stores their profile and credentials and links them to an Access Group. The Operator record is how an individual user is represented in Pega.

Associates an operator with an APPLICATION, a set of ACCESS ROLES, the available PORTALS, and available work pools. The Access Group determines which application, portal, and roles a user receives. A Persona corresponds to an Access Group.
Defines WHAT a user is permitted to do — the permissions to classes and actions (role-based access control, RBAC). Access Roles are granted via the Access Group.

elements.text: Think of a building: the Persona is the job title (e.g., 'Nurse'), the Operator record is your personal employee badge, the Access Group is the badge's programmed profile (which building/app and which doors), and Access Roles are the specific doors (permissions) the badge can open.

bulletPoints: Relationship chain: Persona ↔ Access Group → Access Roles; the Operator record references the Access Group.
Personas determine which work assignments and functionality users can access (work access).
One Persona/Access Group can serve many users with the same needs.

elements.description: Verifies WHO the user is — confirming identity at login (e.g., username/password, SSO, multi-factor). Authentication answers 'Are you really you?' and happens FIRST.

Determines WHAT an authenticated user is allowed to access and do — enforced through Access Roles/Access Groups (RBAC). Authorization answers 'What are you allowed to do?' and happens AFTER authentication.

elements.text: Authentication is showing your passport at the airport (proving who you are); authorization is your boarding pass deciding which gate/seat you may enter (what you're allowed to do). You authenticate first, then you're authorized.

bulletPoints: Authentication = identity verification (login); Authorization = permissions (what you can access).
Authentication comes first; authorization then governs access via roles.
Together they implement the organization's operational and security policies.

examPitfalls.title: User vs. Persona
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A user is one individual; a Persona is a category/role shared by many users.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Individual person → user. Role/category of users with shared access → Persona.

examPitfalls.title: Authentication vs. Authorization
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The classic security trap. Authentication = WHO you are (login); Authorization = WHAT you can do (roles). Order: authenticate first, then authorize.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: AuthN = identity; AuthZ = permissions. Verify identity before granting access.

examPitfalls.title: Access Group vs. Access Role
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Access Group ties an operator to an application, portals, and roles; Access Role defines the actual permissions.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Access Group = the bundle (app + portals + roles + work pools). Access Role = the specific permissions.

examPitfalls.title: Operator record's link
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The Operator record references an Access Group; it is how an individual user is represented and connected to roles/app.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Operator ID → Access Group → Access Roles is the access chain.

examPitfalls.title: Persona maps to an Access Group
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A Persona corresponds to an Access Group (with its roles), which is how role-based access is realized.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Design Personas, then implement them via Access Groups and Access Roles.

examPitfalls.title: Work access comes from the Persona/roles
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Which work and functionality a user can access is governed by their Persona/Access Group/roles, not arbitrary settings.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: To change what work a user can do, adjust their Persona/Access Group and Access Roles.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Fifty customer service representatives all need the same application access and responsibilities. What does this group represent in Pega?

options.text: A single Persona shared by all 50 users
A single Operator record for all 50

practiceQuiz.hint: A Persona is a category or role of users sharing the same access needs and experience goals.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Persona is a category of users sharing the same access needs; all 50 CSRs map to one CSR Persona. Each individual still has their own Operator record.

optionExplanations.A: Shared responsibilities define the CSR Persona.
optionExplanations.B: Different individuals do not require different Personas.
optionExplanations.C: Shared credentials would erase individual operator identity.
optionExplanations.D: Customers are not the staff access category.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What does an Operator record represent, and what does it link to?

options.text: An individual user's profile/credentials, linked to an Access Group
A category of users, linked to nothing

practiceQuiz.hint: An Operator record represents one individual user and links them to their Access Group for permissions.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Operator record represents an individual user — storing their profile and credentials — and links to an Access Group that provides the application, portals, and Access Roles. An Access Role only defines permissions, not the full operator profile.

optionExplanations.A: The operator identifies one user and their access context.
optionExplanations.B: A user category describes a Persona.
optionExplanations.C: A role alone does not provide the operator profile.
optionExplanations.D: A landing page displays content, not user identity.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which artifact ties an operator to an application, available portals, available work pools, and a set of Access Roles?
practiceQuiz.hint: The bundle that points to app + portals + roles.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Access Group associates an operator with an application, one or more portals, available work pools, and Access Roles. An Access Role alone only defines which classes and actions the user is permitted — it does not bundle the full application context.

optionExplanations.A: The Access Group bundles application, portal and role access.
optionExplanations.B: A role supplies permissions within that bundle.
optionExplanations.C: Data mapping does not grant application access.
optionExplanations.D: A queue holds team assignments, not access privileges.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which artifact defines WHAT actions and classes a user is permitted to use (the permissions themselves)?
practiceQuiz.hint: Access Roles define RBAC permissions — specifying which classes and actions a user may perform.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Access Role defines the permissions (role-based access control). The Access Group bundles roles; the Operator record is the individual; the Persona is the role category.

optionExplanations.A: Roles define permissions for application classes.
optionExplanations.B: The group collects roles and application context.
optionExplanations.C: An operator identifies the individual receiving access.
optionExplanations.D: A Persona describes shared user needs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A user logs in with username, password, and a one-time code. Which security concept does this represent?
practiceQuiz.hint: Authentication verifies WHO the user is before the system decides what they are allowed to do.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Verifying identity at login — through credentials, tokens, or MFA — is authentication. Authorization is the separate, subsequent step that governs what the now-authenticated user is permitted to access and do.

optionExplanations.A: Credentials and the one-time code establish identity.
optionExplanations.B: Permissions are a separate access decision.
optionExplanations.C: Field mapping does not verify identity.
optionExplanations.D: A decision table is not a login mechanism.

practiceQuiz.scenario: After a user logs in, Pega checks their Access Roles to decide which Cases and actions they may perform. Which concept is this?

options.text: Authorization (what the user is allowed to do)

practiceQuiz.hint: Authorization determines WHAT an authenticated user is permitted to access and perform.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Determining what an authenticated user may access and do via their assigned roles is authorization. Authentication has already confirmed identity at login; authorization is the next layer that enforces role-based access control.

optionExplanations.A: The check determines permitted actions after login.
optionExplanations.C: Calculating a value does not grant permissions.
optionExplanations.D: A deadline does not authorize case actions.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is explaining the Pega security model to a new team member who is unclear about what happens first when a user logs in. Which sequence is correct for application security?

options.text: Authentication first (verify identity), then authorization (grant access by role)
Both happen only after the Case resolves
Neither is needed if a Persona exists

practiceQuiz.hint: The correct sequence is: first authenticate (verify identity), then authorize (grant access by role).
practiceQuiz.rationale: Authentication verifies identity first; then authorization grants access based on roles. The other sequences or claims reverse this order or conflate the two distinct security layers, which are always applied in this specific sequence.

optionExplanations.A: Verify identity before evaluating application permissions.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses the login security sequence.
optionExplanations.C: Unresolved cases still need access controls.
optionExplanations.D: A Persona does not authenticate its users.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO statements correctly describe the relationship among Personas, Operators, Access Groups, and Access Roles?

options.text: An Operator record references an Access Group
A Persona corresponds to an Access Group that grants Access Roles
An Access Role authenticates the user at login
A Persona is a single individual user

practiceQuiz.hint: Operator → Access Group → Roles; Persona ↔ Access Group.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Operators reference an Access Group, and a Persona corresponds to an Access Group granting Access Roles. Access Roles handle authorization (not authentication), and a Persona is a category, not one individual. No partial credit.

optionExplanations.A: The operator links the individual to an Access Group.
optionExplanations.B: A created Persona has a corresponding access configuration.
optionExplanations.C: Roles grant permissions rather than checking login credentials.
optionExplanations.D: A Persona is a user category.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A manager needs additional permissions to approve high-value Cases. Where is this change most appropriately made?

options.text: Adjust the manager Persona's Access Group/Access Roles to grant the permission
Add a default value to a field

practiceQuiz.hint: Permissions are defined in Access Roles and bundled in the Access Group tied to the user's Persona.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Permissions are governed by Access Roles within the Access Group that is linked to the operator's Persona. Authentication confirms identity, default values pre-fill fields, and Wait Steps pause workflow — none of these grant access permissions.

optionExplanations.A: Approval access belongs in the permission configuration.
optionExplanations.B: Changing login identity checks does not grant approval rights.
optionExplanations.C: Pre-filled values do not authorize the manager.
optionExplanations.D: Waiting changes workflow timing, not permissions.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An organization wants to enforce its operational and security policies in the application. Which Pega capability set is central to this?

options.text: Role-based access control via Personas, Access Groups, and Access Roles, plus authentication/authorization

practiceQuiz.hint: Security policy enforcement uses RBAC (Personas, Access Groups, Access Roles) plus authentication and authorization.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Operational and security policies are enforced through role-based access control — Personas, Access Groups, and Access Roles — combined with authentication and authorization layers. SLAs, routing, and Data Transforms serve process-management purposes.

optionExplanations.A: Identity and access controls enforce the security requirements.
optionExplanations.B: Calculations cannot replace identity and permission checks.
optionExplanations.C: Workflow sequencing does not establish authorized access.
optionExplanations.D: Discussion and alerts do not enforce access policies.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Two different job functions need different application portals and permissions. How should a BA model this?

options.text: Define separate Personas, each backed by its own Access Group (with appropriate portals and Access Roles)
Give both functions one Operator record
Use a single Access Role for everyone

practiceQuiz.hint: Different job roles with different access needs should each be backed by a separate Access Group.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Distinct job functions are modeled as separate Personas, each backed by an Access Group with the right portals and Access Roles. Sharing one Operator/Role or relying on authentication alone won't differentiate access.

optionExplanations.A: Distinct access needs warrant distinct access configurations.
optionExplanations.B: Shared operator identity prevents individual accountability.
optionExplanations.C: One undifferentiated permission set misses the differing needs.
optionExplanations.D: Successful login alone does not distinguish permissions.

quickRecap.value: User = an individual; Persona = a role/category of users sharing access needs (many users → one Persona).
An individual user's profile/credentials; references an Access Group.
Ties an operator to an application, portals, work pools, and Access Roles. A Persona corresponds to an Access Group.
Defines permissions (RBAC) — what classes/actions a user may use; granted via the Access Group.
Verifies WHO you are (login/identity); happens first.
Determines WHAT you can access/do (via roles); happens after authentication.
